thread.title: Target Date Vs. Total Market For Taxable Savings - Vanguard Target Retirement 2040 Fund Inv (MUTF:VFORX)

author: Christopher Price
title: Target Date Vs. Total Market For Taxable Savings - Vanguard Target Retirement 2040 Fund Inv (MUTF:VFORX)
text:
Just last year, I read a book titled I Will Teach You To Be Rich by Ramit Sethi, who is a popular personal finance guru. His book recommends simplifying your financial life by sticking to automatic payments, a single credit card that pays cash back or other rewards, and target date mutual funds.
His reasoning behind investing in a target date fund is the fact that it is diversified and that it should transition over to more conservative and less volatile investments over time. This should theoretically allow for greater growth over the accumulation phase and greater stability and income during the retirement phase.
Another additional benefit of this type of investment is the fact that it will periodically rebalance so that the recommended asset allocation does not get too far out of balance in a lengthy bear or bull market. Furthermore, this rebalancing will take place automatically with no further effort on the part of the investor.
There is much to support this recommendation for those who want to avoid having to make too many decisions regarding their investments.
Another recommendation that's popular, especially among the early retirement segment of the personal finance sphere is a fund that tracks the total US stock market. For example, JL Collins recommends Vanguard's Total Stock Market Index Fund ( VTSAX ). This fund includes every publicly traded company in the US, whether the company happens to be a mega-cap stock like Amazon ( AMZN ) or Apple ( AAPL ) or companies that have very small market caps.
Both should provide growth over the long run. VTSAX should provide more growth, however, as there will be no bonds involved. On the other hand, a target date fund should have a little bit less in the way of volatility because of its exposure to bonds. This volatility should get lower over time as the targeted asset allocation comes to include more bonds and cash holdings.
There are a number of different target date funds, as they tend to be focused around a five-year period that should be close to a person's possible retirement date. This particular analysis will focus on Vanguard's Target Retirement 2040 Fund ( VFORX ), which is the fund that tracks closes to my estimated retirement date.
Fund Holdings When comparing VFORX and VTSAX, the Vanguard site is clear, but the number of holdings may seem a bit small when looking at the target date fund. The Target Retirement 2040 Fund has a total of four funds listed. These funds include both domestic and international equity and bond funds. The bond funds make up slightly more than 15 percent of the investments in VFORX, and domestic equities from VTSAX make up just above 50 percent of the fund's holdings.
VTSAX, on the other hand, lists many more holdings. It attempts to track the entire US stock market, and as such has 3,639 companies. These are all held in VFORX, as well. There are no bonds held in the total stock market fund, so investors who want to diversify into income investments might want to check out Vanguard's Total Bond Market Index Fund ( VBMFX ) or a similar fund from another brokerage.
Both VFORX and VTSAX provide a great deal of diversification.
Expenses From a management fee perspective, the Total Stock Market Index Fund comes out ahead with a very small management fee of 0.04 percent. This compares to the fees of 0.15 percent when looking at the Total Retirement Fund. It should be noted that the latter fund's expense ratio may go down slightly over time, as the Total Retirement 2020 Fund ( VTWNX ) has fees of 0.13 percent.
Neither of these fees is excessive, but they do add up over time. Therefore, those who want to cut down on fees would obviously do better with VTSAX in that regard.
Taxes Those who invest in either of these funds in a qualified retirement fund will not have to worry about taxes on an annual basis unless they are making withdrawals. Holdings within a Traditional or Roth IRA allow for tax-free growth and dividends. When withdrawn at a "traditional" retirement age, the only taxes due would be normal income taxes on a traditional account, and these would depend upon the tax rate of the retiree. Roth distributions, as long as they happen after age 59.5 are tax-free because the government views the tax as having been paid up front before the money got invested in the fund.
Those who hold these accounts in a taxable account, on the other hand, may have to worry about a tax bill at the end of the year. Both VTSAX and VFORX pass on dividends to their owners. The Total Stock Market Index Fund pays out on a quarterly basis, while the Target Retirement 2040 fund pays out on an annualized basis.
These dividends would be taxable like any others. Qualified dividends are taxed between 0 and 20 percent, while non-qualified dividends are taxed at the marginal rate . This could reach 37 percent for very high earners.
Additionally, investors have to pay capital gains taxes on these funds. Over the past several years, VTSAX has paid nothing to investors in capital gains distributions. This means that the capital gains tax would be $0. The current turnover ratio for VTSAX is a small 3 percent.
On the other hand, investors in VFORX have seen both short-term and long-term capital gains over the past four years. These are taxable. The long-term gains are taxed between 0 and 20 percent, depending upon a person's tax bracket. The short-term gains are taxed at the marginal rate, which can, again, reach as high as 37 percent as of 2018. The turnover rate on VFORX, according to Seeking Alpha's analysis is 8 percent , which means that more of this fund's holdings could be taxable in a given year.
These tax bills should admittedly be quite small in the early years of an investment journey, but they could grow quite a bit as the holdings grow over time with price increases and additional investments.
Conclusion The additional fees and capital gains on Vanguard's Target Retirement 2040 Fund make it less advantageous for those who are looking to save on taxes in a taxable account. The more stable holdings of VTSAX mean that capital gains are less likely, which should slightly cut down on the amount of tax that an investor would need to pay. While the total amount of tax might be negligible on VFORX, few people would want to pay the tax. Of course, those who are concerned with possible (even likely) volatility around their retirement dates will likely appreciate the automatic rebalancing that will take place with an investment in the Target Retirement 2040 Fund. Additionally, according to the home pages of each of the funds, a $10,000 investment in VTSAX ten years ago would have been worth more than $34,700 as of December 31, 2018. A similar investment in VFORX at the same time would only be worth $26,551, which is a difference of more than $8,000.
